title: Salivary Gland Disease: Parotitis and Salivary Stones
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains the three common causes of a swollen salivary gland: mumps parotitis, acute bacterial parotitis, and an obstructing salivary stone. Each follows from normal gland structure and function. Mumps is a blood-borne viral infection of ductal tissue that also reaches the testis, pancreas, and meninges. Bacterial parotitis is an ascending infection that takes hold when salivary flow falls. Stones form where saliva is thick and drains slowly, which is why they favor the submandibular gland. Board questions give the patient, the side, the duct finding, the timing of pain, and the amylase and lipase, and ask you to name the process and predict its complications.

connections.how: Amylase comes from both the salivary glands and the pancreas, so lipase is needed to tell parotitis from pancreatitis.
Mumps orchitis shows how swelling inside the unyielding tunica albuginea causes tubular necrosis and testicular atrophy.
Mumps is a classic cause of aseptic (viral) meningitis with a lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid.
Sjogren syndrome destroys salivary acini, lowers flow, and so predisposes to ascending bacterial parotitis, while vaccination has made mumps uncommon.
The organisms of bacterial parotitis and secondary sialadenitis are oral and skin flora that ascend the duct when flushing stops.

terms.def: Inflammation of the parotid gland, from viral infection, bacterial infection, or obstruction.
Inflammation of any salivary gland, often from infection that ascends a duct when salivary flow is reduced or blocked.
Formation of a calcified stone (sialolith) inside a salivary gland or its duct.
The parotid duct, which crosses the masseter, pierces the buccinator, and opens opposite the upper second molar.
The submandibular duct, which runs forward and upward through the floor of the mouth to open at the sublingual papilla beside the lingual frenulum.
A cluster of secretory cells that produce a watery, protein-rich fluid containing enzymes such as salivary amylase.
A cluster of secretory cells that produce mucins, which make saliva thick and viscous.
The mumps envelope protein that binds sialic acid on host cells and cleaves it to release new virions.
The amylase isoenzyme made by salivary glands; it is measured together with pancreatic amylase in total serum amylase.
Inflammation of the testis; in mumps it is caused by viral spread through the blood after puberty.
Meningitis with a lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid and no bacteria on Gram stain or culture, usually caused by a virus.
Painful swelling of an obstructed gland that begins when eating stimulates secretion and settles as secretion slows.

sections.title: Mumps parotitis versus acute bacterial parotitis

blocks.text: The parotid is the largest salivary gland and is purely serous, so its saliva is watery and rich in salivary amylase. It lies over the mandibular ramus in a dense fascial capsule. Steady salivary flow protects it by flushing Stensen duct and delivering lysozyme, lactoferrin, and secretory IgA.
Mumps parotitis: a blood-borne viral infection

Mumps virus is an enveloped, nonsegmented, negative-sense single-stranded RNA paramyxovirus with one serotype. Its hemagglutinin-neuraminidase (HN) protein binds sialic acid on host cells and its fusion (F) protein merges the envelope with the cell membrane. Spread by droplets, it replicates in upper airway epithelium and regional lymph nodes, and a viremia then seeds glands and meninges after an incubation of about 16 to 18 days.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of mumps
steps: Replication in epithelium and regional lymph nodes
Ductal infection with edema and lymphocytes
blocks.caption: One viremia explains why mumps can involve salivary glands, gonads, pancreas, and meninges.

blocks.text: Infected ductal epithelium degenerates and the interstitium fills with edema, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages. There is no neutrophilic exudate, so the duct opening may be red but expresses no pus. Swelling stretches the capsule, causing pain on chewing and earache. It is bilateral in most cases, though it often begins on one side. Injured acini release salivary amylase into the blood, so total serum amylase rises while lipase, made only by the pancreas, stays normal unless the pancreas is also infected.

Orchitis affects roughly a quarter to a third of infected postpubertal males, usually one testis; edema inside the unyielding tunica albuginea compresses seminiferous tubules, causing pressure necrosis and later atrophy, although sterility is rare. Mumps also causes oophoritis, pancreatitis, aseptic meningitis with a lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid (sometimes without parotitis), and usually unilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
Acute bacterial parotitis: an ascending infection

Bacterial parotitis is an ascending infection: when salivary flow falls, oral bacteria climb Stensen duct. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common isolate; streptococci and anaerobes also occur. Every major risk factor lowers flow or blocks the duct: dehydration, older age, the postoperative period, anticholinergic and diuretic drugs, Sjogren syndrome, poor oral hygiene, and a duct stone. Neutrophils fill ducts and acini with pus, which gland massage pushes out of the duct opening. The unilateral gland is hot and very tender in its tight capsule, with fever and neutrophilic leukocytosis. An abscess can spread into the deep neck spaces.

blocks.title: Mumps parotitis compared with acute bacterial parotitis
blocks.caption: Pus at the duct in a low-flow host points to bacteria; bilateral swelling with gonadal, pancreatic, or meningeal disease points to mumps.

blocks.title: Worked example: amylase versus lipase in parotid swelling
blocks.text: An unvaccinated 19-year-old has fever of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F), bilateral preauricular swelling, and mild epigastric discomfort. Amylase is 410 U/L (reference about 30 to 110 U/L); lipase is 40 U/L (reference about 10 to 60 U/L). Step 1: total amylase includes salivary and pancreatic isoenzymes, and inflamed parotid acini leak the salivary one. Step 2: lipase is pancreatic and normal, so pancreatitis is not supported; lipase above about three times its upper limit would suggest it. Step 3: amylase cannot separate viral from bacterial parotitis; the host, side, and duct finding do.

blocks.predict: A dehydrated 78-year-old on an anticholinergic drug develops one hot, tender parotid after surgery. What will gland massage produce?
blocks.explain: Low flow stops duct flushing, so oral bacteria, most often Staphylococcus aureus, ascend and cause neutrophilic inflammation; pus exits the duct.

sections.title: Why salivary stones favor the submandibular gland, and what obstruction causes

blocks.text: The submandibular gland is mixed, mostly serous with some mucous acini, and supplies most resting saliva. Its deep part wraps around the posterior border of the mylohyoid into the floor of the mouth. Wharton duct, about 5 cm long, runs forward and upward from there, crossed by the lingual nerve, to open at the sublingual papilla beside the lingual frenulum.

blocks.title: The major salivary glands and their stone risk
blocks.caption: The gland with thicker saliva and an uphill duct forms most stones.

blocks.text: A stone (sialolith) starts as an organic nidus of mucin, shed cells, or debris on which calcium phosphate, mostly hydroxyapatite, precipitates in layers. Two kinds of factors favor the submandibular gland. Chemically, its saliva has more mucin and so is more viscous, it is more alkaline, which lowers calcium phosphate solubility, and it carries more calcium than parotid saliva. Mechanically, Wharton duct is long, rises against gravity when upright, bends around the mylohyoid, and ends at a narrow orifice, so slow flow gives crystals time to grow. Parotid stones are fewer and more often radiolucent; most submandibular stones are radiopaque.

blocks.title: How a submandibular stone forms
steps: Slow flow up a long, rising duct
Mucin and debris form a nidus
blocks.caption: Chemistry supplies the material and duct mechanics supply the time.

blocks.text: Obstruction hurts when secretion is stimulated. Between meals, slow secretion seeps past a partial block. Food triggers a parasympathetic surge: acetylcholine on M3 receptors raises acinar Ca2+ and drives chloride and water secretion. The acini secrete against the blocked duct, pressure rises, and the encapsulated gland swells painfully within minutes of starting a meal (salivary colic), then settles as secretion slows. Swelling is unilateral, an anterior stone may be felt in the floor of the mouth, and blood tests are normal.

blocks.title: Obstruction and infection feed each other
steps: Stagnant saliva stops flushing the duct
blocks.caption: Stasis invites infection, and the scarring it leaves worsens stasis.

blocks.text: Stagnant saliva lets bacteria, most often Staphylococcus aureus, ascend and cause secondary bacterial sialadenitis: constant pain, fever, redness, and pus at the papilla. Repeated episodes cause chronic sialadenitis with duct dilation, fibrosis, and acinar atrophy, leaving a firm gland that can mimic a tumor.

blocks.title: Worked example: predicting the course of a duct stone
blocks.text: A 45-year-old notes swelling below the left mandible within minutes of starting lunch that fades over an hour. Step 1: meal-linked pain means secretion against an obstruction. Step 2: the site is the submandibular gland, the usual stone site. Step 3: predict a tender gland at meals, a stone palpable in the floor of the mouth, normal blood counts, and little flow from the left papilla. Step 4: constant pain with fever of 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) and pus at the papilla would mean secondary bacterial sialadenitis.

blocks.predict: Why does a Wharton duct stone hurt most at the start of a meal rather than during sleep?
blocks.explain: Eating triggers a parasympathetic surge of secretion against the blocked duct, so pressure rises in the encapsulated gland; during sleep secretion is minimal.

integration.text: Anatomy and histology set the pattern of disease. The serous parotid sends a thin, amylase-rich saliva down a short duct, while the mixed submandibular gland sends thicker, calcium-rich saliva up a long duct, which is why stones favor the submandibular gland. The dense parotid capsule explains the pain of both kinds of parotitis, and the facial nerve inside the gland is usually spared by infection. Physiology links the conditions: salivary flow is a host defense, so anything that lowers it (dehydration, anticholinergic drugs, Sjogren syndrome, or a stone) opens the duct to ascending bacteria.

Microbiology and pathology separate the causes. Mumps reaches the gland through the blood and provokes mononuclear inflammation, so it is often bilateral and spreads to the testis, pancreas, meninges, and cochlea; bacteria reach the gland up the duct and provoke neutrophilic inflammation, so the disease is usually unilateral with pus at the duct. These are patterns, not rules: mumps can begin on one side, other viruses can cause parotitis, and amylase rises in any parotitis, so the duct finding and the host carry more weight than any single test.

summary: The parotid is purely serous and drains by Stensen duct opposite the upper second molar; the submandibular gland is mixed and drains by Wharton duct at the sublingual papilla.
Mumps is an enveloped negative-sense RNA paramyxovirus that spreads by droplets and reaches glands and meninges through viremia.
Mumps parotitis is often bilateral, with mononuclear inflammation and no pus at the duct.
Parotitis raises total serum amylase from the salivary isoenzyme; a normal lipase means the pancreas is spared.
Mumps orchitis after puberty is usually unilateral; swelling inside the tunica albuginea causes tubular necrosis and atrophy, but sterility is rare.
Acute bacterial parotitis, most often Staphylococcus aureus, ascends Stensen duct when salivary flow falls, as in dehydrated, older, or postoperative patients.
Pus expressed from the duct on gland massage indicates bacterial infection.
About 80 to 90% of salivary stones form in the submandibular gland because its saliva is thicker, more alkaline, and richer in calcium, and its duct is long and rises against gravity.
A duct stone causes painful swelling at meals that settles afterward; constant pain with fever means secondary bacterial sialadenitis.

verify: Frequency figures vary between sources: bilateral parotid involvement in mumps (about two thirds to three quarters), subclinical or nonparotid infection (about one third), and orchitis in postpubertal males (quoted from about 15% to 30%); confirm the values NABNE expects.
Mumps incubation is given as about 16 to 18 days, with a range of about 12 to 25 days; confirm the figure NABNE uses.

The distribution of salivary stones (about 80 to 90% submandibular, about 5 to 10% parotid, sublingual rare) and the statement that most submandibular stones are radiopaque while parotid stones are more often radiolucent vary among series.
The share of resting saliva from the submandibular gland (about two thirds) and the rise in the parotid share with stimulation are quoted differently in physiology texts.
Amylase and lipase reference ranges in the worked example are approximate and depend on the laboratory and assay.
The current ICTV genus name for mumps virus is Orthorubulavirus (formerly Rubulavirus); confirm which name NABNE uses, since this chapter gives only the family.
Some texts note that mumps meningitis can occasionally lower cerebrospinal fluid glucose; this chapter states only the lymphocytic pleocytosis. Confirm whether this exception is tested.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Stensen duct and Wharton duct or only the descriptive terms parotid duct and submandibular duct.
